title: Your first token on Ethereum, built in one evening

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On March 11, 2024, a classroom at ÉTS turned into a tiny economy. Everyone in the room had created their own token, and they were sending it to each other.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Wait, a whole room of beginners deployed a token in one night?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That was Byzantium's first Ethereum workshop, led by Khalil Anis Zabat, and Antoine was there to recap it. Beginners and more advanced people all went home having deployed something real.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you even start? Ethereum sounds like a lot of setup.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's why it began in Remix, which runs in the browser. You compile and deploy a contract without installing anything, so you can redo it at home. Then came a local setup with an editor and node tooling, the way professionals repeat the process.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And where does the token live? You don't want to spend real money in a classroom.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right, they used Sepolia, a test network. You grab free test ETH from a faucet, use MetaMask as your wallet, and an Infura-style service as the bridge to the network.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does the code look like? Is it intimidating?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's tiny. The trick is OpenZeppelin, a shared library of standards. Instead of rewriting how transfers work, the contract inherits a proven ERC-20 token. You just choose a name, a symbol, the decimals, and an initial supply minted to whoever deploys it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's like ordering a car from a catalog and picking the color, rather than building the engine.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's a good way to see it. Then the fun part: people copied each other's contract addresses and sent tokens around until the room felt like a mini economy.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And when you look up a transaction afterward?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You open a block explorer and every transaction is a row: who sent what, to whom, how much gas, which block. Until you see that line, Solidity is just syntax. Afterward, it's a public ledger with your address on it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Did questions come up beyond the basics?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A few good ones. Gas keeps contracts from looping forever. The ABI tells apps which functions a contract offers. And big data usually stays off-chain, with just a hash or link stored on the chain.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Byzantium plans follow-ups on other token types and deeper Solidity. This evening was the on-ramp. The full write-up has the contract code and photos from the room.
